IntentTwin: Deconfounding Candidate Support
and the Oracle-to-Deployment Gap
in Offline Web Behavior Prediction

Miaobo Hu Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China Affiliation: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China*Corresponding author: xiaojun@ucas.ac.cn    Shuhao Hu Affiliation: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China*Corresponding author: xiaojun@ucas.ac.cn    Xiaobo Guo Affiliation: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China*Corresponding author: xiaojun@ucas.ac.cn    Xin Wang Affiliation: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China*Corresponding author: xiaojun@ucas.ac.cn    Bokun Wang Affiliation: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China*Corresponding author: xiaojun@ucas.ac.cn    Daren Zha Affiliation: Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China*Corresponding author: xiaojun@ucas.ac.cn    Jun Xiao Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China
Abstract

Offline web-behavior benchmarks frequently insert the demonstrated action into a finite candidate set and then measure reranking. We show that this protocol can create a candidate-support confound: when the target is outside training support while all distractors are sampled from that support, support membership identifies the gold action without modeling behavior. We formalize this effect with support-identifiability rate (SIR), construct support-balanced candidate sets, and evaluate a target-free dual-path proposer that combines support retrieval with open-vocabulary DOM/LM proposals.

On filtered OPeRA (4,282/469/992 train/dev/test steps), the original protocol has SIR 1.00001.0000 on target-OOV rows and a support-only rule reaches 1.00001.0000 OOV Exact@1. Support balancing reduces SIR to 0.00000.0000; the strongest conditional reranker obtains 0.72140.7214 overall Exact@1, 0.79880.7988 on IV rows, and 0.56680.5668 on OOV rows. The target-free dual-path system reaches Proposal Recall@16 0.69150.6915 and end-to-end Exact@1 0.52120.5212, compared with oracle conditional Exact@1 0.74500.7450. On Mind2Web, the same audit yields SIR 0.23800.2380 and an oracle-to-proposal gap of 0.21250.2125. A 200-row semantic audit labels 0.71500.7150 of exact-key OOV targets as semantically novel, 0.24500.2450 as locator/string variation, and 0.04000.0400 as ambiguous (Cohen’s κ=0.8173\kappa=0.8173). These measurements show why support composition must be controlled alongside candidate accuracy when offline results are used to reason about deployment.

1 Introduction

Web interaction traces contain a prefix of observations and actions, but an offline benchmark often supplies the gold action as an item in the candidate set. Consider a target such as click “Blue 256GB”. In an oracle evaluation it is guaranteed to appear among 15 distractors; in deployment, a system must first discover and name that action from the current page and history. Ranking correctness is therefore conditional on candidate availability.

A second issue appears when candidate availability is correlated with the evaluation label. In the original target-anchored construction, the logged action is inserted into the candidate set while every negative is sampled from the frozen training vocabulary. For a target-OOV row, the gold action is thus the unique out-of-support candidate. A support-only rule can identify the target from candidate membership alone; we call this candidate-support confounding. We therefore separate behavioral discrimination from the information revealed by the support composition of the candidate set.

We study this distinction with a target-free context ctc_{t} and a structured action key at=(type,target,value)a_{t}=(\mathrm{type},\mathrm{target},\mathrm{value}). The protocol freezes the candidate support using training targets, keeps sessions disjoint, and stores an ordered row ledger containing candidates, probabilities, ranks, NLLs, and provenance. A test target whose exact key is absent from the training support is marked target-OOV; it is never added to the training vocabulary or the model input.

We organize the study around four questions:

  1. 1.

    Support confounding: When does candidate membership reveal the gold action independently of the behavioral context?

  2. 2.

    Deconfounded reranking: How do rankers behave when IV and OOV candidates are support-balanced?

  3. 3.

    Oracle-to-deployment gap: What changes when the oracle anchor is replaced by a target-free proposer?

  4. 4.

    Support-aware proposal: Can context-gated retrieval and open-vocabulary proposal improve coverage without candidate-level gates?

Our contributions are:

  • •

    a formal candidate-support confound and the support-identifiability rate (SIR) diagnostic;

  • •

    a support-balanced candidate protocol with exact action-key strata, pseudo-OOV calibration, and complete candidate-level ledgers; and

  • •

    a target-free dual-path proposal evaluation that reports proposal recall, covered reranking, and end-to-end exact action selection on OPeRA and Mind2Web.

2 Related Work

Offline decision modeling.

Maximum-entropy inverse reinforcement learning (MaxEnt IRL) models a demonstration as a distribution over trajectories rather than as a deterministic label (Ziebart et al., 2008). Our scorer uses a finite conditional candidate-level softmax objective rather than a trajectory partition function. We therefore refer to this family as factorized candidate scoring below; some implementation artifacts retain the historical “IRL” label. The objective is an IRL-inspired finite-choice energy surrogate: it does not solve a trajectory-level inverse problem, occupancy-matching problem, or reward- identification problem. Offline RL methods address distribution shift by constraining learned values to the support of logged data, with implicit value learning providing a useful reference point for our candidate-ranking setting (Levine et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2020; Kostrikov et al., 2022). Dataset and protocol design are central to offline evaluation, as emphasized by D4RL (Fu et al., 2021). Diffusion-based trajectory models offer a complementary way to represent multi-step behavior, but their offline gains depend strongly on the quality of the latent and action interfaces (Janner et al., 2022). We borrow the probabilistic decision view while making the candidate support and preference factors explicit.

Web and tool-using agents.

ReAct interleaves reasoning and acting (Yao et al., 2023), while Toolformer and Reflexion study tool use and verbal feedback (Schick et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023). WebArena and Mind2Web provide realistic browser tasks and traces (Zhou et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2023); AgentBench broadens evaluation across agent environments (Liu et al., 2024). These benchmarks motivate our focus on action semantics and session-level context. Mind2Web in particular uses candidate generation and top-kk recall, whereas our narrower contribution is the train-only candidate contract, row-level likelihood ledger, and explicit target-OOV analysis for a closed-choice factorized scorer.

Preference learning and explanations.

Direct preference optimization and human-feedback fine-tuning (Rafailov et al., 2023; Ouyang et al., 2022) are useful future baselines for our language-model arm, whereas the present mainline isolates a symbolic candidate scorer. Self-Refine and Voyager show how feedback and self-generated memory can improve agent behavior (Madaan et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023); our focus is the preceding measurement contract that makes such improvements auditable. Finally, the faithfulness literature warns against treating textual rationales as explanations without independent validation (Turpin et al., 2023).

3 Method

3.1 Evaluation contract and candidate support

Let a session be a sequence of observed steps τ=(o1,a1,…,oT,aT)\tau=(o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{T},a_{T}), where each action ata_{t} is serialized as an action type and a structured target. For a prediction row at time tt, the context ctc_{t} contains only the prefix observations and actions, mode-selected identity fields (user ID and/or persona when enabled), and metadata available before ata_{t}. The target ata_{t} is excluded from ctc_{t}. We score a candidate set 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t} of size 16 and report

pθ​(a∣ct)=exp⁡(Rθ​(ct,a)/β)∑a′∈𝒜texp⁡(Rθ​(ct,a′)/β),β=0.5.p_{\theta}(a\mid c_{t})=\frac{\exp(R_{\theta}(c_{t},a)/\beta)}{\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}_{t}}\exp(R_{\theta}(c_{t},a^{\prime})/\beta)},\qquad\beta=0.5.

The central distinction is between the action support available to a scorer and the action that was logged. Let

Vtrain={(type,target,value)​ keys observed in ​Dtrain}.V_{\mathrm{train}}=\{(\mathrm{type},\mathrm{target},\mathrm{value})\text{ keys observed in }D_{\mathrm{train}}\}.

An evaluation row is IV when its exact target key is in VtrainV_{\mathrm{train}}, and target-OOV otherwise. For example, ranking a logged “Blue 256GB” click among supplied alternatives tests conditional reranking; deployment must first propose and name that target. Ranking correctness is therefore conditional on candidate availability. The negative-action vocabulary is frozen from training action keys. For each row, the logged target is inserted once as an evaluation anchor and 15 deterministic negatives are drawn from that vocabulary; the configured ratio selects up to eight hard negatives (sharing the action type or target when possible) and seven random non-duplicates, with a deterministic small-pool fallback. Thus a test target outside the training vocabulary is scoreable but marked target-OOV: it does not update the global vocabulary or supply input context. This target-anchored design has 100% candidate-anchor coverage by construction and evaluates conditional reranking under a controlled choice set; it is not open-vocabulary action generation. The evaluator inserts the logged target only after the model has formed the target-free context, so the reported Top-kk values measure conditional reranking given an oracle candidate anchor rather than the probability of proposing that action in deployment.

The builder deduplicates the train action vocabulary by the (type,target,value)(\mathrm{type},\mathrm{target},\mathrm{value}) key before sampling. With 16 slots and a hard-negative ratio of 0.5, it requests up to eight same-type or same-target negatives and fills the remainder with random train-vocabulary actions. A SHA-256 digest of session_id:step_id:seed initializes the per-row RNG, and a small pool falls back to unused hard negatives without duplicating the anchor. This makes the candidate list byte-reproducible while exposing a controlled source of difficulty: the held-out rows contain 777 click rows with 15 same-type negatives, 65 with 14, 3 with 13, 107 input rows with two, and 40 terminate rows with none. The resulting frozen train vocabulary contains 1,280 unique action keys; its digest is retained in the split statistics and every run receipt.

Support identifiability and balanced candidates.

For a candidate set 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t}, let I(a)=𝟙[a∈Vtrain]I(a)=\mathbb{1}[a\in V_{\mathrm{train}}]. The support-identifiability rate (SIR) is the fraction of rows for which the gold candidate is the unique candidate with its support status. The support-only baseline observes I⁡(a)I(a) and selects that unique candidate, breaking ties by the frozen frequency order. To remove this cue, the support-balanced protocol fixes qq out-of-support candidates and 16−q16-q in-support candidates in every set, with q∈{1,2,4,8}q\in\{1,2,4,8\}; q=4q=4 is the primary setting. Balanced candidates preserve the action-type hard-negative ratio and use the same deterministic row seed.

3.2 Three evaluation regimes

The same target-free context is evaluated under three deliberately different information contracts. (1) Oracle candidate reranking inserts the logged target into a fixed 16-way set and measures Top-1, NLL, MRR, exact-action accuracy, action-type accuracy, and Macro-F1. (2) Closed-vocabulary proposal removes the target anchor and original candidate list, then ranks the complete frozen VtrainV_{\mathrm{train}}; Recall@kk and Exact@1 measure the proposal boundary, and target-OOV recall is structurally zero. (3) Observation recoverability extracts named actions from the current serialized observation without reading the target or source candidate list. Its coverage is an information ceiling, not a learned generator. We never multiply metrics across regimes: each number is conditional on its own candidate and observation assumptions.

3.3 Data protocol

We use the filtered OPeRA protocol (Wang et al., 2025): 394/43/90 session-disjoint train/dev/test sessions and 4,282/469/992 steps. The test split contains 661 IV and 331 target-OOV rows (845 click, 107 input, and 40 terminate). Users recur across splits, so the primary claim is session-level generalization rather than unseen-user transfer. A deterministic user-disjoint stress test (3,799/1,419/525 rows; 187 target-OOV test rows) is retained only as a secondary diagnostic. All paper-facing claims use the session-disjoint split unless stated otherwise.

3.4 Information timing

The target-free context flows through the model; the demonstrated action enters only the training loss or the held-out evaluator after that context is formed. Train-fitted vocabularies, candidate lists, and optional segmentation or representation artifacts are frozen before dev/test. Every held-out row retains its ordered candidates, probabilities, rank, NLL, and provenance hashes.

3.5 Scorers and support-aware hybrid

The protocol-matched Candidate-CE control maps target-free context and canonical action features to one scalar logit per candidate. Factorized conditions use the same 16-way softmax but parameterize the score as R⁡(c,a)=w​(c)⊤​q​(c,a)R(c,a)=w(c)^{\top}q(c,a) with a train-frozen 14-factor bank and lightweight hash features. These coordinates are auditable model states, not identified or human-validated preferences; implementation details and secondary probes are reported in Appendix A.

The observed IV/OOV trade-off motivates a gate that uses no held-out targets. Combining a target-free prior sprior​(c,a)s_{\mathrm{prior}}(c,a) with a candidate-ranker score gives

shyb(c,a)=sprior(c,a)+αg(a)srank(c,a),g(a)=𝟙{countDtrain(a)≥m}.s_{\mathrm{hyb}}(c,a)=s_{\mathrm{prior}}(c,a)+\alpha g(a)s_{\mathrm{rank}}(c,a),\qquad g(a)=\mathbb{1}\{\mathrm{count}_{D_{\mathrm{train}}}(a)\geq m\}.

For the reported diagnostic, m=1m=1: an action key is in-support if it appears at least once in the training split. The gate therefore uses only training support counts and does not inspect the held-out target. We withhold 20% of training action keys as pseudo-OOV keys, fit the gate and α\alpha without test targets, and score the held-out test split once. This is a diagnostic of support-aware interpolation, not a claim of open-vocabulary generation.

Finite-choice objective.

The scorer optimizes finite-choice cross-entropy, optionally with smoothness, hierarchy, and masked rationale penalties. This is an IRL-inspired energy surrogate rather than trajectory-level MaxEnt IRL: it has no trajectory partition function, occupancy matching, reward identification, or sequential credit assignment. Every inference row retains its ordered candidates, probabilities, rank, NLL, stratum, and run hashes.

4 Experiments

4.1 Setup and evaluation protocol

Reproducible setup.

All conditions use the same session-disjoint filtered OPeRA split, frozen 16-way candidate lists, target-free prompts, and train-only support artifacts. Factorized controls use three epochs, learning rate 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}, gradient accumulation 16, temperature 0.5, and seeds 13,42,202613,42,2026. The QLoRA reference uses Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with 4-bit adapters on qprojq_{\mathrm{proj}} and vprojv_{\mathrm{proj}}, rank 16, three epochs over all 4,282 training rows, and 2,048-token training contexts. All six full-budget adapters have complete 992-row ledgers under both the matched 384-token held-out evaluator and the 2,048-token full-context evaluator. The matched evaluation and detailed receipts are in Appendix A; the full-context persona follow-up is a separate single-condition aggregate. No test row is used for model selection, and completion NLL is not compared with candidate-softmax NLL.

Metrics.

We report candidate Top-1, target NLL, MRR, exact-action accuracy, action-type accuracy, Macro-F1, and IV/OOV strata. Candidate Top-1 equals exact-action accuracy because the target is inserted as an anchor. Where multiple seeds are available, means ±\pm sample SD are computed across training seeds; single-seed rows are shown without dispersion. Row-level ledgers and clean run metadata bind every reported aggregate.

4.2 Support confounding and balanced reranking

The original target-anchored protocol makes support membership observable at the candidate level. Every target-OOV row contains one OOV gold action and 15 in-support negatives, so the support-only baseline obtains OOV Exact@1 1.00001.0000 by construction. We report SIR together with behavioral scores to separate this shortcut from context-sensitive ranking.

Support balancing reduces SIR from 1.00001.0000 to 0.00000.0000 on target-OOV rows and reduces the support-only OOV score to 0.25380.2538. The QLoRA reranker retains 0.56680.5668 OOV Exact@1 and 0.72140.7214 overall Exact@1, showing that the deconfounded protocol still measures context-dependent discrimination.

4.3 Support-balance sensitivity

We vary the number qq of out-of-support candidates while fixing the candidate budget at 16. The q=4q=4 setting is primary; the sweep tests whether the observed ranking changes are tied to one candidate composition.

Increasing qq removes the unique-OOV cue while preserving the fixed candidate budget. Overall Exact@1 changes from 0.74290.7429 at q=1q=1 to 0.72140.7214 at q=4q=4 and 0.69510.6951 at q=8q=8; the corresponding OOV values are 0.59800.5980, 0.56680.5668, and 0.52740.5274.

4.4 Target-free proposal and end-to-end action prediction

We remove the demonstrated action and the source candidate list. The proposal stage compares train-frequency retrieval, support retrieval, DOM-copy proposal, constrained QLoRA generation, a fixed union, and the context-gated dual path. Conditional Exact@1 is computed only when the proposal contains the exact target; E2E Exact@1 uses all 992 rows.

The context-gated dual path obtains Proposal Recall@16 0.69150.6915 and E2E Exact@1 0.52120.5212, improving over support retrieval by 0.21970.2197 and 0.18250.1825 respectively. Its OOV E2E score is 0.45620.4562, while support-only retrieval has zero OOV E2E success because its vocabulary is frozen to training keys.

4.5 Ablating the dual-path proposer

The ablation keeps the proposal budget at K=16K=16 and changes only the source and allocation rule. The full dual path has the highest R@16, E2E, and OOV E2E; the context gate without the language-model path gives the highest IV E2E (0.53400.5340).

4.6 Cross-benchmark audit on Mind2Web

We apply the same decomposition to the official cross-task, cross-website, and cross-domain splits. The audit reports support-identifiability, oracle conditional ranking, target-free proposal coverage, covered reranking, and end-to-end exact selection.

SIR rises from 0.18360.1836 on cross-task to 0.29240.2924 on cross-domain, while E2E Exact@1 falls from 0.48690.4869 to 0.39900.3990. The same ordering of proposal and oracle metrics is preserved across splits.

4.7 Semantic audit of exact-key OOV

Exact structured keys provide an auditable support definition but can separate locator or string variants of one semantic action. Two annotators reviewed a stratified sample of 200 exact-key OOV rows without model predictions and adjudicated disagreements.

The audit labels 0.71500.7150 of rows as semantically novel and 0.24500.2450 as locator/string variation, supporting exact-key OOV as a conservative but interpretable audit variable.

4.8 Reliability after support deconfounding

We recompute calibration and selective-risk metrics for the original anchor, support-balanced, and target-free protocols. This separates confidence information from confidence induced by candidate support.

The support-balanced protocol increases ECE from 0.06380.0638 to 0.07590.0759 and AURC from 0.12140.1214 to 0.13980.1398, exposing the calibration cost of removing the support cue. The target-free pipeline has the highest residual uncertainty, with AURC 0.25270.2527 and Error AUROC 0.68340.6834.

4.9 Context truncation sensitivity

The same seed-13 adapter was evaluated with three truncation policies. Exact@1 is 0.68470.6847 for left truncation, 0.10960.1096 for right truncation, and 0.71830.7183 for head–tail truncation. The non-monotonic response makes token-retention policy an explicit part of the evaluation contract.

4.10 Language-model reference

The three-seed 2,048-token no-persona QLoRA reference reaches 0.7399±\pm0.0044 overall Top-1, 0.8164±\pm0.0089 on IV rows, and 0.5871±\pm0.0194 on target-OOV rows; its MRR is 0.8081±\pm0.0031. Under the same full-context protocol, the three-seed persona aggregate reaches 0.7093±\pm0.0056 overall, 0.7993±\pm0.0071 on IV rows, and 0.5297±\pm0.0194 on target-OOV rows (MRR 0.7757±\pm0.0039). The lower persona values are a descriptive secondary control, not evidence of a causal persona effect or a superiority claim. Both rows are conditional reranking references, not open-vocabulary proposal results. The full table, including action type and completion NLL, and the matched 384-token protocol are reported in Appendix A.

As a context-sensitivity diagnostic, we also scored the same seed-13 no-persona adapter on the identical 992-row test ledger at five measured held-out prompt limits between 256 and 2,048 tokens. This isolates evaluation truncation under a fixed trained adapter; it is not a causal estimate of training context length. The complete directional sweep is reported in Appendix A without interpolation between measured limits. The measured curve is non-monotonic: exact-action accuracy reaches 0.7450 at 2,048 tokens but falls to 0.0968 at 1,024 tokens, while the corresponding OOV values are 0.5952 and 0.1662. We therefore treat the sweep as a diagnostic of protocol sensitivity rather than evidence that longer context is uniformly better.

4.11 Limitations

The primary OPeRA split is session-disjoint with recurring users, and exact-key support is a lexical audit variable. The Mind2Web audit covers official cross-task, cross-website, and cross-domain splits; it measures candidate coverage and ranking rather than online browser interaction. The released protocol records candidate composition, support status, proposal provenance, and row-level hashes so future work can extend the audit to additional DOM-grounded proposers.

5 Conclusion

We identified candidate-support confounding in target-anchored offline web evaluation: when OOV targets are paired with in-support distractors, support membership alone reveals the gold action. SIR and the support-only baseline make this shortcut directly measurable. Support-balanced candidates reduce SIR to 0.00000.0000 and retain context-sensitive OOV ranking at 0.56680.5668 Exact@1.

The target-free dual-path proposer reaches Proposal Recall@16 0.69150.6915 and end-to-end Exact@1 0.52120.5212, exposing an oracle-to-deployment gap of 0.22380.2238. The same decomposition transfers to Mind2Web, where SIR ranges from 0.18360.1836 to 0.29240.2924 across the official splits. These results establish candidate support as an evaluation variable that belongs beside accuracy, proposal coverage, and reliability in offline web-behavior studies.

AI-use Statement

We used generative AI tools for language polishing and summarizing references. We have not used generative AI tools to generate experimental results, create synthetic datasets, formulate mathematical claims, provide proofs, or make decisions regarding research conclusions. The design of the methodology, experimental setup, analysis, and interpretation of results were conducted and verified by the authors. Other required disclosure tasks not mentioned above are not applicable to this work. We take full responsibility for the final content of this work, including all text, claims, analyses, and artifacts produced with the assistance of generative AI tools.

ETHICS STATEMENT

The traces contain interaction histories and may encode sensitive preferences. The study uses de-identified offline data, applies data minimization and access control, and reports aggregate metrics with row-level provenance for auditability. We release code and derived metadata under the applicable data and software licenses and exclude private browsing content.

REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT

The Supplementary Material contains the code, configuration files, frozen splits, candidate ledgers, proposal outputs, evaluation scripts, and run manifests needed to reproduce the reported tables and figures. It also records the three training seeds, deterministic candidate-generation rule, model and tokenizer identifiers, hardware settings, and SHA-256 hashes for generated artifacts. The OPeRA and Mind2Web data remain subject to their original licenses and access procedures.

Appendix A Evaluation Protocols and Artifact Contracts

The paper-facing tables below report the mean and standard deviation across the three factorized-scoring training seeds where such aggregates are available; the 2,048-token QLoRA table has a three-seed no-persona aggregate and a separate three-seed persona aggregate. They omit long confidence- interval strings so that the values remain readable. The matched six-arm table uses 384-token held-out truncation with the same full training budget. Cells marked “–” are unavailable by design, not zeros. The complete generated ledgers, including 95% intervals and every stratum, remain in the machine-readable supplementary tables and the machine-readable supplementary ledger.

A.1 Implementation details and secondary protocols

The legacy factorized scorer uses deterministic 256-dimensional hash features and a train-frozen bank of K=14K=14 lexical factors. Its candidate vector is qψ​(c,a)=tanh⁡(MLPψ​[H⁡(c);H⁡(a)])+e⁡(a)q_{\psi}(c,a)=\tanh(\mathrm{MLP}_{\psi}[H(c);H(a)])+e(a) and its hierarchy uses R⁡(c,a)=w​(c)⊤​q​(c,a)R(c,a)=w(c)^{\top}q(c,a), with population, user, session, and optional segment terms. The registered smoothness, hierarchy, and masked-rationale coefficients are 10−210^{-2}, 10−310^{-3}, and 11; the constant L1L_{1} term is disabled. The factor coordinates are context-conditioned score features, not identified preferences.

The optional surprise interface is trained only on training transitions, with lag-1 boundaries constrained to lengths [2,12][2,12]. Its clean four-arm audit does not show a consistent neighborhood advantage. Semantic caches, identity controls, rationale ablations, and frozen-checkpoint interventions are reported only as directional diagnostics. None supplies human factor labels, causal browser effects, or open-vocabulary generation evidence.

A.2 Full proposal algorithm and edge cases

The target-free pipeline is evaluated as one executable contract. Retrieval and open proposal are generated from the same target-free context, deduplicated by the exact action key, and merged before conditional reranking. The logged target is used only to compute recall and exact-action outcomes after proposal generation.

Empty proposal sets are counted as proposal failures and receive E2E Exact@1 zero; they are retained in the denominator. Duplicate structured keys keep the first occurrence from the stable merge. Ties use the frozen frequency order, then lexical action-key order. These rules make Recall@kk, covered reranking, and E2E accuracy composable across seeds and benchmark splits.

A.3 Metric definitions and aggregation

For a row with target ata_{t} and proposal list PtP_{t}, proposal Recall@kk is 𝟙[at∈Pt(k)]\mathbb{1}[a_{t}\in P_{t}^{(k)}]. Covered Exact@1 is evaluated on rows where at∈Pta_{t}\in P_{t}, whereas E2E Exact@1 uses all rows. The oracle-to-deployment gap is the difference between oracle conditional Exact@1 and E2E Exact@1 on the same split. SIR uses only support indicators and is independent of model scores.

Means and sample standard deviations are computed across training seeds when the full ledger is available. For split-level audits, rows are the aggregation unit and each split keeps its own denominator. Session bootstrap intervals in the later appendix section resample complete sessions; they describe session variation and complement seed variation. All reported decimals use four places and zero is reserved for a measured zero rather than an unavailable entry.

A.4 Artifact schema and provenance fields

Every row in the released ledgers is keyed by a session identifier, step identifier, and deterministic seed. The schema keeps the target key separate from the target-free input, records the candidate source and support flags, and stores the scorer output before aggregation. This separation allows the same row to be audited under the original, balanced, and target-free contracts.

The provenance fields also record invalid-action handling and tie resolution. Aggregation scripts consume only rows whose run receipt and input hashes pass verification; this keeps unavailable artifacts distinct from measured zeros and preserves the denominator for every reported metric.

The formal full-context language-model diagnostic is listed separately because its token-level objective is not numerically comparable to the factorized-scorer candidate likelihood. Both no-persona and persona rows aggregate complete seeds 13,42,202613,42,2026 under the same 2,048-token evaluator. The completion score is retained for within-arm diagnostics only; it must not be read as calibrated candidate probability.

Appendix B Language-Model and Context Diagnostics

B.1 Persona full-context support-aware diagnostic

The following single-seed supplement combines the complete persona SFT prior ledger with a support-only persona ranker. The prior uses the 2,048-token full-context evaluator; the ranker uses a 1,024-token training and evaluation context. Both ledgers retain the same 16-way candidates and target-free contexts, but the different context budgets preclude a matched-context comparison with the no-persona hybrid or the persona 384-token hybrid. The weight is selected on the independent 874-row pseudo-OOV calibration ledger. The candidate Softmax NLL for the prior is recomputed from its 16-way probabilities and is not its QLoRA completion NLL.

B.2 Matched full-budget SFT with 384-token evaluation

The complete six-arm aggregate is the paper-facing descriptive matched-protocol aggregate for the language-model diagnostic. Every arm uses the same filtered split, candidate lists, training budget, and seed-matched evaluation seed. The evaluator uses max_length=384, row batch size 1, shared prompt context, mean completion normalization, and target-free prompts. Training still uses context 2,048, so the table is an evaluation-truncation comparison rather than a 384-token training experiment. The machine-readable report retains per-row records, source report hashes, checkpoint manifests, and the clean run receipt.

B.3 A1 segment-context control

The available matched A1 aggregate adds only frozen, train-calibrated segment metadata to the target-free prompt. All six arms use the same 2,048-token training budget and the same 384-token held-out evaluator, candidate lists, and seed-matched evaluation protocol. The segment-context control is markedly below the no-segment full-context reference and is therefore retained as a negative control, not as evidence that the learned boundaries improve action selection. It also does not validate the boundaries as human subgoals.

B.4 Persona support-aware 256-token diagnostic

For completeness, we retain the latest fixed-weight persona support result. The prior is the complete 2,048-token persona ledger and the support-only ranker is trained and evaluated with a 256-token context. The support gate uses only train action-key counts; α=0.1\alpha=0.1 is fixed rather than selected on the held-out test set. The result is therefore directional and asymmetric with respect to context budget.

B.5 Context truncation sensitivity

The context-length comparison below keeps the adapter, train/test split, candidate lists, target-free prompt, scoring normalization, and evaluation seed fixed. We evaluate five held-out prompt limits, 256256, 384384, 768768, 1,0241{,}024, and 2,0482{,}048 tokens; only the held-out prompt limit changes. The result therefore measures sensitivity to evaluation truncation for one trained adapter rather than a training-context ablation. Every point covers the complete 992-row test split and remains directional. We do not interpolate between measured limits or treat this sweep as evidence about training with a different context length.

Appendix C Target-Free Proposal and Transfer Audits

C.1 Target-free proposal and observation-space audits

The oracle-anchor protocol is intentionally separated from target-free proposal evidence. As a supplementary boundary diagnostic (explicitly boundary diagnostic), we removed the gold action and the source 16-way list, then ranked the complete frozen train vocabulary with the anchor-trained Candidate-CE checkpoint. Table 19 reports proposal recall and end-to-end exact selection. Because the scorer was trained only on target-anchored 16-way examples, this full-vocabulary pass is a closed-vocabulary extrapolation rather than a learned open-vocabulary generator; target-OOV recall is therefore structurally zero. It is retained for auditability and must not be read as a proposal benchmark.

The proposal diagnostic still assumes that the observation serialization contains enough information to name an actionable target. We therefore ran a separate observation-only audit that extracts named DOM elements from the current HTML and treats every non-empty name as an upper-bound click candidate. It recovers 536/992 targets (0.5403): click 429/845 (0.5077), input 107/107 (1.0000), and terminate 0/40 (0.0000). The 456 unrecovered rows are an observation recoverability ceiling, not model failures; the audit is marked boundary diagnostic because the filtered HTML does not expose a complete action space. The paired machine-readable receipts retain the full row order, source hashes, and missing-target examples in the supplement.

The bounded Mind2Web OPeRA-dynamics probe is below its matched random dynamics control on cross-task (0.8567 versus 0.8594), cross-website (0.8420 versus 0.8445), and cross-domain (0.8612 versus 0.8628) splits. It is therefore a negative offline action-type diagnostic, not evidence of representation transfer; candidate-element ranking, an official MindAct comparison, and online browser validation were not run.

Appendix D Representation and Intervention Diagnostics

D.1 Rationale, representation, and intervention diagnostics

The matched seed-42 rationale-loss ablation changes only the masked rationale loss weight. The identical Top-1 values and the small NLL/MRR changes provide no evidence of a ranking gain, and the lexical rationale audit contains only 11 rows with explicit factor evidence. These values are a model-ranking diagnostic, not a human explanation-validity test.

The native-scale representation and intervention checks are intentionally kept separate. Dynamics and centroid probes predict action types, the VQ probe exhibits codebook collapse, diffusion reports noise loss without decoded actions, and the counterfactual row measures frozen-checkpoint sensitivity.

D.2 Stratification, cases, and factor elasticity

The complete 992-row seed-13 ledgers expose the main failure mode: action-type prediction is often correct while the structured target is wrong. The action-type/vocabulary table, candidate-composition figure, and session summaries are descriptive views of the target-anchored protocol; QLoRA remains a separate directional language-model diagnostic rather than a capacity-matched factorized-scorer comparison.

The machine-readable report, ordered records, and clean run receipt for this audit are retained as the supplementary artifact hierarchy_diagnostics_a3_s13. The report covers the same candidate set and SFT likelihood cache as the A3 table above, so the diagnostic does not introduce a second evaluation protocol.

Representative records show exact matches, type-preserving misses, and type mismatches. The rows are selected deterministically from the complete ledger; shortened paths are included only for readability and do not add semantic labels.

For the clean frozen factorized checkpoint (artifact-labeled “IRL”), candidate-intervention sensitivity (CIS) is the total-variation response after appending preregistered factor evidence; preference elasticity (PES) is the change in expected factor evidence per unit weight edit; and semantic orthogonality (SOS) is the off-diagonal/diagonal elasticity ratio. CIS 0.0382, PES 0.0005, SOS 1.0643, and sign accuracy 0.4347 indicate small, poorly isolated responses. They characterize this scorer, not causal behavior in people or browsers.

The retained SFT-integrated probes provide a further, explicitly exploratory check of the proposed composition. A3 adds the hierarchical preference head to the segment-conditioned SFT likelihood prior; A4 adds an IRL-inspired finite-choice candidate objective; and A5 adds the masked rationale loss. On the same seed-13 992-row split, A4 reaches 0.5343 Top-1 and A5 reaches 0.5333, while the OOV Top-1 values are 0.1390 and 0.1360. The small decrease for A5 is consistent with the matched generic rationale ablation and is not evidence against weak supervision in general. Because these artifacts use the generic evaluator and do not satisfy the strict component-aware A0–A8 manifest, they are reported only as supplementary directional probes in Table 27.

Paired A3/A4 and semantic-OOV post-hoc diagnostics.

The complete paired ledger separates the apparent A4 improvement into vocabulary strata. A4 gains Top-1 on 148 of 661 IV rows and loses on 37, whereas it gains on only 8 of 331 OOV rows and loses on 94. The resulting Top-1 changes are +0.1679+0.1679 for IV and −0.2598-0.2598 for OOV, while the overall change is only +0.0252+0.0252; A4’s target NLL falls by 1.0336 on IV but increases by 0.1020 on OOV. Input and terminate rows are 100% Top-1 for both arms, so this is not evidence that the candidate-difficulty mix changed between arms. These paired values make the IV-dominated trade-off explicit without assigning it to an SFT-prior mechanism.

The same report stratifies the semantic rows using target-string properties computed after evaluation. On the session-disjoint split, semantic CE has OOV Top-1 0.01510.0151 (5/331); the normalized target-length buckets are 0.08700.0870 (23 rows) for 1–32 characters, 0.02380.0238 (84) for 33–64, and 0.00450.0045 (224) for 65+. Its nearest-train token-overlap buckets are 0/0.0270/0.0149 for (0,0.25](0,0.25], (0.25,0.5](0.25,0.5], and >0.5>0.5, respectively, so the sparse direction is not monotone. The user-disjoint semantic CE arm is 0/187 in every displayed bucket; the corresponding semantic factorized scorer values are 0.0211 and 0.0160 on the two splits. Because these are target-derived lexical proxies with small buckets, they cannot establish a failure mechanism, semantic interpretability, or open-vocabulary generalization. The complete paired and bucket summaries, together with upstream hashes, are retained in the supplementary artifact “review_diagnostics_s13”.

To complement the seed-level standard deviations in the provisional factorized-scorer aggregate, we also resample the complete held-out sessions in the seed-13 ledgers. The resulting percentile intervals are descriptive row means under session dependence, not confidence intervals over users or training seeds. Figure 9 and Table 29 report the same 90-session bootstrap for the directional hierarchical factorized-scorer and full-context QLoRA ledgers.

Appendix E Calibration and Selective Risk

E.1 Candidate composition and calibration diagnostics

The target-anchored evaluator fixes the target in every 16-way choice set, but the number of same-type negatives still changes the difficulty of the conditional ranking problem. Table 31 reports the candidate slots aggregated by target action type. These counts describe the evaluation contract; they are not additional training examples.

Candidate probabilities are also evaluated as probabilities rather than only as ranks. Figure 10 shows reliability curves for the target probability, while Table 32 reports two ten-bin expected calibration errors (ECEs) and the multiclass Brier score. Target-pp Top-1 ECE bins the probability assigned to the gold target and compares it with whether that target is ranked first; it is a target-anchored diagnostic, not the usual multiclass confidence ECE. Max-confidence ECE instead bins the largest candidate probability and compares it with whether the argmax candidate is correct, which is the standard max-confidence multiclass summary. These diagnostics use the same complete 992-row seed-13 records and should not be read as evidence that the QLoRA token objective is comparable to the factorized-scorer candidate NLL. Our multiclass Brier convention is the per-row sum over all 16 candidate classes, averaged over rows: 1N∑i∑j(pi​j−𝟙[j=yi])2\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\sum_{j}(p_{ij}-\mathbb{1}[j=y_{i}])^{2}. The supplementary JSON also retains the candidate-count-scaled mean of the same squared errors, but the paper table reports the multiclass sum convention.

E.2 Selective risk and failure detection

To test whether the retained candidate probabilities support a post-hoc abstention diagnostic, we compute a risk–coverage curve from the same complete 992-row seed-13 ledgers. A row is correct exactly when its predicted candidate equals the target; confidence is the maximum candidate probability. Rows are accepted in descending confidence order, and Risk@50% is the error rate among the highest-confidence half of each stratum. AURC is the trapezoidal area under the realized prefix curve, while Error AUROC scores 1−maxj⁡pi​j1-\max_{j}p_{ij} against the binary top-1 error event.

This is a target-anchored conditional-reranking diagnostic, not an online utility estimate, a learned abstention policy, or an open-vocabulary proposal test: the demonstrated target remains inserted into every candidate set. Table 33 shows that the factorized scorer is selectively useful on in-vocabulary rows but fails on target-OOV rows (AURC =0.9342=0.9342, Risk@50% =0.9096=0.9096, and Error AUROC =0.5426=0.5426). The QLoRA ledgers retain stronger OOV error detection in the available seed-13 comparison. The added support-aware rows make the utility boundary explicit: the no-persona hybrid reaches Risk@50% =0.0101=0.0101 overall and 0.00000.0000 on target-OOV rows, but its OOV stratum has no errors so Error AUROC is undefined; the persona 384/384 hybrid has OOV Risk@50% =0.1145=0.1145 and Error AUROC =0.8047=0.8047. These are separate, target-anchored conditional reranking diagnostics (the no-persona prior/ranker use 2,048/1,024 tokens and the persona pair uses 384/384), not matched comparisons or deployment-time abstention results. This is a single-seed directional diagnostic; it does not establish open-vocabulary reliability. The machine-readable reports and clean run receipts are retained as the machine-readable selective-risk audit files.

Reproducibility receipt.

The review diagnostic bundle is derived without retraining. It contains six ordered ledgers: paired A3/A4 ledgers over 992 session-disjoint rows, two semantic ledgers over the same 992 rows, and two semantic ledgers over the 525 user-disjoint rows. The session-disjoint target-vocabulary split is fixed at 661 in-vocabulary versus 331 target-OOV rows; the user-disjoint split is registered separately in its own receipt. The machine-readable the machine-readable review-diagnostic audit files bundle records source/output hashes, upstream report/record/run metadata, and the clean Git state used to materialize the summaries.
